clue.text: Chronicle of mass migration of vermin

definitions.text: Chronicle of mass migration of vermin

parts.words: Chronicle of mass migration of vermin
parts.note: the 'vermin' are rabbits, and the chronicle is Richard Adams's novel of a warren's flight to a new home on the Hampshire downs

explanation.surface: A dry history of a plague of rats on the move.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Adams's 1972 novel follows a band of rabbits leaving their doomed warren to found a new one.

clue.text: English poet may be a dreamer (all wet)

indicators.note: the letters of the following words may be turned into something else, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: An English poet is gently mocked as a hopeless, soggy dreamer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be' is the anagram signal: the fourteen letters of A DREAMER and ALL WET are rearranged into the poet's full name.
explanation.definitionFit: Walter de la Mare (1873-1956) was an English poet and writer of ghost stories, best known for 'The Listeners'.

clue.text: Number of days that Rose Macaulay wrote in 1919

definitions.text: Number of days that Rose Macaulay wrote in 1919

parts.words: Number of days that Rose Macaulay wrote in 1919
parts.note: Rose Macaulay published a collection of poems in 1919 whose title is a count of days

explanation.surface: A question of how long a novelist spent writing one year.
explanation.definitionFit: Rose Macaulay's 1919 volume of poems was titled 'Three Days', so the number is a small digit.

clue.text: "Government with the engine of a lawn-mower and the brakes of a—. " (Jonathan Lynn and Sir Anthony Jay)

definitions.text: "Government with the engine of a lawn-mower and the brakes of a—. " (Jonathan Lynn and Sir Anthony Jay)

parts.words: "Government with the engine of a lawn-mower and the brakes of a—. " (Jonathan Lynn and Sir Anthony Jay)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from the writers of the BBC sitcom Yes Minister, contrasting a feeble engine with luxury brakes

explanation.surface: A satirical quotation about government from the authors of Yes Minister.
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation contrasts a weak motor with the brakes of a famously grand British luxury car marque.

clue.text: Underprivileged eponymous Hemingway type?

parts.note: Hemingway's novel 'To Have and ...' is named after the poor half of its pairing, so such a person is eponymous

explanation.surface: A question about a poor character type in Hemingway.
explanation.definitionFit: A poor person lacking wealth or privilege, as in Hemingway's title 'To Have and Have Not'.

clue.text: Controversy revealing Chopin, perhaps, on the road to first concerto

parts.note: the composer Chopin was Polish, an example of a Pole
the M1 is Britain's first motorway, written MI in crosswords

indicators.note: the word first asks for the opening letter of concerto

explanation.surface: A musical controversy about Chopin travelling to his first concerto.
explanation.walkthrough: In this down clue 'on' means sitting above; the road is the M1, Britain's London-to-Leeds motorway, written with an I in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A polemic is a fierce written or spoken attack, a piece of argument and dispute.

clue.text: Some Cambridge fellow encourages poet

indicators.note: some of the letters of the words fellow encourages, so a run is taken from inside them

explanation.surface: A Cambridge don cheers on a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' means only part of 'fellow encourages' is used: the run straddling the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilfred Owen was the First World War poet of 'Dulce et Decorum Est'.

clue.text: It bore stamps of both Watt and Auden

definitions.text: It bore stamps of both Watt and Auden

parts.words: It bore stamps of both Watt and Auden
parts.note: the 1936 GPO documentary film directed by Harry Watt, with verse by W. H. Auden, about a postal train carrying stamped letters

explanation.surface: A thing marked with the impress of an engineer and a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watt' suggests James Watt and steam, but it is Harry Watt, the film's co-director.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1936 film followed the overnight postal train from London to Scotland, with Auden's poem as commentary.

clue.text: Charging a tenor, perhaps, for plainsong

indicators.note: perhaps tells us these letters could form something else, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A choir charges a tenor a fee for singing plainsong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' is the anagram signal on all fourteen letters of CHARGING A TENOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Plainsong is unaccompanied liturgical chant of the Western church, traditionally linked to Pope Gregory I.

clue.text: Droll love tangle of ballad hero

indicators.note: a tangle mixes things up, so the letters of droll and love are jumbled

explanation.surface: A comic love tangle befalls the hero of an old ballad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tangle' is the anagram signal on DROLL and LOVE together.
explanation.definitionFit: The traditional Child ballad tells of the knight who rides away from Lady Nancy Belle and returns to find her dead.

clue.text: He was a cold as poor Tom

definitions.text: He was a cold as poor Tom

parts.words: He was a cold as poor Tom
parts.note: in King Lear, Gloucester's son disguises himself as the mad beggar Poor Tom, who cries 'Tom's a-cold'

explanation.surface: Someone felt chilly while pretending to be a pauper named Tom.
explanation.definitionFit: In King Lear, Gloucester's legitimate son disguises himself as the beggar Poor Tom on the heath.

clue.text: Hermia's father in Privilege Usurped

indicators.note: the answer sits in the words Privilege Usurped, straddling them

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean father's authority is usurped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points inside 'Privilege Usurped', where the name runs across the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: In A Midsummer Night's Dream, the Athenian Egeus demands his daughter Hermia marry Demetrius.

clue.text: No one can identify the sea captain …

definitions.meaning: Jules Verne's commander of the submarine Nautilus

explanation.surface: Nobody can recognise the mysterious skipper.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this clue to the next, which also names a fictional figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for nobody, it is also Jules Verne's captain of the Nautilus.

clue.text: … the way Silver identifies young buck

parts.note: ST abbreviates street, a way
AG is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: Long John Silver spots a young deer by its path.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silver' suggests Long John Silver of Treasure Island, but it is the element silver, chemical symbol AG.
explanation.definitionFit: A male deer, and also a young man out on the town without women.

clue.text: "A—- —is a confirmed guest" (Damon Runyon)

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Damon Runyon about a visitor who never pays his way

explanation.surface: A Runyon quip about a guest who never leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: A sponger who lives off others' hospitality is, in Runyon's words, a permanent guest.

clue.text: Dicey Runyon character in the city

definitions.meaning: Nathan, the gambler who runs a floating crap game in Guys and Dolls, based on Runyon's stories
the Michigan city famous for car-making

explanation.surface: A gambling character from Runyon turns up in town.
explanation.definitionFit: Nathan Detroit runs the dice game in Guys and Dolls, and the name is also the Michigan motor city.

clue.text: Precarious situation of Bagley's men

parts.note: Desmond Bagley wrote the thriller 'The ... Men', whose title names a precarious walkway

explanation.surface: Characters in a Bagley thriller find themselves in peril.
explanation.definitionFit: A high wire is a byword for a precarious position, and Bagley's 1973 thriller is 'The Tightrope Men'.

clue.text: Lead role in pirated version of Byron?

definitions.text: Lead role in pirated version of Byron?

parts.words: Lead role in pirated version of Byron?
parts.note: Byron's narrative poem about the pirate Conrad has a title naming its hero's trade; 'pirated' hints at the seafaring robber

explanation.surface: A question about the star part in a bootleg Byron edition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pirated' suggests an unauthorised copy, but it points to the title hero being a sea-raider.
explanation.definitionFit: Byron's 1814 poem 'The Corsair' has as its hero a buccaneer, a sea-raider.

clue.text: Verifiable characteristic of Ayer's empiricism

parts.note: A. J. Ayer championed the verification principle of the philosophical school known as ... positivism or empiricism

explanation.surface: A philosophy student describes Ayer's theory as testable.
explanation.definitionFit: Ayer's school was logical positivism, also called logical empiricism, built on the verification principle.

clue.text: Behold poet becomes harness-maker

parts.note: LO is an old word meaning look or behold
a rimer is a variant spelling of rhymer, a versifier

explanation.surface: Lo, a poet takes up a trade making horse tack.
explanation.definitionFit: A lorimer is a craftsman making bits, spurs and metal fittings for horse bridles.

clue.text: That of Donne was seen as a marriage temple

definitions.text: That of Donne was seen as a marriage temple

parts.words: That of Donne was seen as a marriage temple
parts.note: Donne's poem argues that an insect which has bitten both lovers is 'our marriage bed, and marriage temple'

explanation.surface: Donne's poem treats something as a sacred wedding place.
explanation.definitionFit: In Donne's poem the insect that has sucked both lovers' blood is called 'our marriage bed, and marriage temple'.

clue.text: Philippino to label a record

parts.note: a tag is a label
a log is a written record, as a ship's log

explanation.surface: A Filipino sticks a label on a vinyl record.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tagalog are a people of Luzon in the Philippines, and their language underlies Filipino.

clue.text: Old flame attracts Dream character

parts.note: a flame draws in a night-flying insect, and one of Titania's fairies in A Midsummer Night's Dream bears that insect's name

explanation.surface: A former lover lures a figure from a dream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old flame' suggests an ex-lover, but it is a literal flame that draws the insect.
explanation.definitionFit: A fairy attending Titania in A Midsummer Night's Dream is named after the insect drawn to lamps.

clue.text: Frenchman in Aristophanes play?

definitions.meaning: derogatory British slang for a native of France
Aristophanes wrote a comedy whose chorus is of croaking amphibians

explanation.surface: A Frenchman acts in a Greek comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a French person, and the croaking creature of the chorus in Aristophanes' comedy 'The Frogs'.

clue.text: One among Horatio's rich friends

indicators.note: the name is found among the letters of the words Horatio's rich

explanation.surface: A courtier counted among Horatio's wealthy circle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'among' points inside 'Horatio's rich', and the whole clue also describes the foppish courtier of Hamlet's court.
explanation.definitionFit: Osric is the affected courtier in Hamlet who referees the final duel, one of the Danish court Horatio moves in.

clue.text: His name alone invites perusal of his work

definitions.text: His name alone invites perusal of his work

parts.words: His name alone invites perusal of his work
parts.note: the Victorian novelist's surname sounds like a command to look through his books

explanation.surface: An author whose very name tells you to open his books.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Reade was the Victorian novelist of 'The Cloister and the Hearth', his surname echoing the verb for perusing.

clue.text: "Among the most noisome of the —s and dens of London" (Oliver Twist)

definitions.text: "Among the most noisome of the —s and dens of London" (Oliver Twist)

parts.words: "Among the most noisome of the —s and dens of London" (Oliver Twist)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Dickens, where the missing word is an old term for a brothel or squalid haunt

explanation.surface: A Dickens line about London's foulest haunts.
explanation.definitionFit: In old usage the word meant a brothel or low den, alongside its kitchen sense of a slow-cooked dish.

clue.text: "The structure of a play is always the story of how the birds come home to — " (Arthur Miller)

definitions.text: "The structure of a play is always the story of how the birds come home to — " (Arthur Miller)

parts.words: "The structure of a play is always the story of how the birds come home to — " (Arthur Miller)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Arthur Miller playing on the saying about chickens and consequences

explanation.surface: Arthur Miller on how plays show consequences returning.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom about chickens coming home to perch means past deeds catching up with someone.

clue.text: Lurid piece made moral, in a way

indicators.note: in a way says the words are made moral only in another arrangement, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sensational play is given a moral ending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a way' is the anagram signal on MADE MORAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A melodrama is a sensational play with exaggerated characters and lurid plotting.

clue.text: He reached breaking point in 1907

parts.note: the critic and publisher's reader wrote a play titled 'The Breaking Point', banned by the Lord Chamberlain and published in 1907

explanation.surface: Someone snapped under pressure in 1907.
explanation.definitionFit: The influential publisher's reader and critic wrote the play 'The Breaking Point', refused a licence and published in 1907.
